frameworks.name: Sphere of Competence Investing Filter
frameworks.definition: A decision rule (attributed by Hormozi to Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger) that restricts investment activity to domains where the investor has deep, practiced expertise; outside those domains, capital losses are predictable.

frameworks.name: Push vs. Pivot Dichotomy
frameworks.definition: A two-branch decision framework for hard entrepreneurial moments: push means intensify effort on the current path because the fundamentals are sound; pivot means change direction because the original assumption was wrong. The critical failure mode is doing neither.

frameworks.name: Partner Contribution Screen
frameworks.definition: A three-criterion test for evaluating potential business partners: the partner must bring time, money, or skills that the founder genuinely lacks. If none of the three is present, the partner is not needed and should not receive equity.

frameworks.name: Backyard Football Fundamentals
frameworks.definition: A strategic heuristic (shared with Hormozi by a private-equity CEO) that warns against complex, clever strategies in favor of relentless execution of a few core basics: acquire customers, deliver excellently, repeat.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the further he operates outside his core sphere of competence (marketing, sales, acquisition, pricing, product), the more money he loses, and the closer he stays to that core, the more money he makes. He uses this pattern to argue that entrepreneurs who already know how to generate wealth should create more wealth rather than divert capital into investment vehicles they do not deeply understand.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: entrepreneur already generates income from a core business competency
investment vehicle is outside that competency domain
claims.mechanism: In unfamiliar domains the investor cannot evaluate quality, detect fraud, or time entry/exit, so adverse selection and information asymmetry systematically transfer wealth to informed counterparties.
bounded_by: does not apply to specialists who have spent years developing competency in a given asset class (e.g., real estate investors, fund managers)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi lost approximately $500,000 in Bitcoin/Ethereum in 2021 after entering near the peak at $60,000 Bitcoin. He characterizes this as gambling, not investing, because he had no analytical framework to evaluate the asset and entered primarily because a friend was entering simultaneously.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: position sized at roughly one month's income at the time

numbers.axis: crypto entry price and loss amount

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that whenever a large group believes something is a good idea, it is usually a bad idea. He uses FOMO (fear of missing out) as a reliable contrarian signal: the feeling of urgency to enter an opportunity is a reliable indicator to pause rather than act.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: When broad consensus forms around an opportunity, the easy money has typically already been captured by early movers; late entrants face compressed upside and full downside.
bounded_by: early entry before consensus forms may genuinely be exceptional; the risk is that an early-stage opportunity looks indistinguishable from a coming fraud

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's rule for evaluating any investment opportunity someone recommends is to require that the recommender has been in the deal for at least two to three years before Hormozi will consider it. Anything shorter than that he disregards entirely, regardless of the persuasiveness of the pitch.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: passive investment outside Hormozi's core competency
claims.mechanism: Early-stage participants have not yet experienced a full cycle of a deal; hold-period less than two to three years leaves open the possibility of favorable conditions that have not yet reversed.

numbers.axis: minimum hold period before recommendation is credible

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's preference for co-investment is to only enter a deal alongside the person actively executing it, not as a passive outside investor. His revised rule: he will buy a property only if the person selling it is also buying the same property with his own money.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: passive investment outside founder's core domain
claims.mechanism: Aligned economic incentives (the seller or operator holds the same risk) ensure the operator has material reason to perform; misaligned incentives allow the operator to profit from fees or spread regardless of investor outcome.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi identifies the necessary and sufficient conditions for a business partnership: the partner must bring at least one of three things the founder lacks — time, money, or skills. If the partner brings none of those, that person is not needed in the business and should not receive equity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: A partner who duplicates the founder's contribution adds no incremental value but extracts proportional equity, reducing the founder's return per unit of work and incentivizing conflict when contributions diverge.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that equity loss is most severe on day one: founders who split equity at launch give away the largest share of future value before the business has demonstrated any returns, and this loss is permanent. The emotional cost of equity conversations day one is far smaller than the financial cost of imbalanced equity at scale.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Equity not reclaimed at founding cannot be recaptured without expensive buyouts or dissolution; early under-negotiation compounds through every subsequent valuation event.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that needing a function in a business (e.g., accounting, legal) does not require giving equity to the person who performs that function. Most business functions can be purchased from vendors, contractors, or fractional specialists without issuing equity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Equity should reflect irreplaceable core-value contribution (customer acquisition or delivery); commodity functions that can be sourced from the market at market rates carry no equity premium.
bounded_by: exception: a technical co-founder in a software business may be irreplaceable and equity-deserving because the core value generation is technical

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that if the business cannot function without the founder but can function without a specific partner, the founder is needed and the partner is not — and the equity split should reflect that asymmetry. Being the rainmaker (the person who brings in all the customers) justifies a disproportionate share of proceeds.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: one party is the primary customer-acquisition driver

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a business owner who takes no salary while claiming to reinvest in growth is most likely not reinvesting — the business is simply not generating profit. The diagnostic question is: what is the return on invested capital? If the founder cannot answer that, the money is not being reinvested; it is being lost.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that every business expense should produce a measurable return on invested capital (ROIC). For small businesses, the minimum acceptable ROIC is 3-to-1, and 5-to-1 to 10-to-1 is achievable because small operators can acquire leads far more cheaply than large organizations can.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: small business with below $5M revenue where founder has direct visibility into unit economics
claims.mechanism: Small operators face no bureaucratic overhead in procurement, can buy leads cheaply, and test rapidly; scale removes those efficiency advantages.
bounded_by: does not apply to brand or relationship investments with long attribution windows

claims.text: Alex Hormozi reports that upgrading his second gym location from a 5,000 sq ft warehouse (opened for $37,000) to a 7,000 sq ft retail anchor location (opened for $250,000) produced identical monthly revenue to the first location. He concludes that the premium spend produced zero incremental return.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: fitness studio in a retail anchor center vs. warehouse-behind-auto-shop
bounded_by: does not mean premium locations never matter; applies specifically when the marginal revenue from location upgrade is zero

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that a fractional improvement in product quality (e.g., from 4.4 to 4.7 stars on Amazon in the same category) can produce a 10x difference in sales volume, meaning incremental quality improvement on the core product dominates all other marketing and operational investments.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: commodity-adjacent marketplace with visible ratings (e.g., Amazon product category)
claims.mechanism: Buyers use rating as a proxy for quality; small rating differences translate to large purchase-probability differences because buyers systematically choose the higher-rated option.

numbers.axis: product rating vs. relative sales volume

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when a founder is too far removed from operational departments — not knowing what problems each department is actively struggling with — they lose the ability to detect costly decisions being made without their knowledge. He calls this knowing where the bodies are buried.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has delegated operational management to department heads
claims.mechanism: Without one-level-deeper knowledge of each department's active problems, a founder cannot recognize when a subordinate has created a large recurring liability (e.g., unauthorized pay raises, runaway legal fees) until the damage has already compounded.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's HR director at Gym Launch unilaterally ordered a cost-of-living study and implemented a company-wide pay raise, adding $600,000 per year in payroll with zero incremental productivity. Hormozi attributes this directly to being too far removed from the HR department to detect the decision in progress.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: annual payroll cost added with zero incremental output

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's undirected compliance mandate at Gym Launch produced $1.2 million per year in legal fees (approximately $120,000 per month) without any compliance improvements being implemented. Four lawyers reviewed every piece of marketing content and held bi-weekly meetings, but none of the resulting notes were read or acted upon.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder delegated compliance to a team that interpreted the mandate literally and outsourced to an external law firm
claims.mechanism: When a budget owner is spending someone else's money (Uncle Alex's money) without accountability for ROI, spending inflates to fill available approval tolerance.

numbers.axis: monthly legal spend with zero compliance output

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that software businesses require a technical co-founder because only someone with genuine software expertise can hold an external development vendor accountable: ensuring code is documented, auditing billing, keeping the codebase transferable, and preventing progressive margin erosion through fee increases.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: software product where core value is generated by proprietary code
claims.mechanism: An outsourced dev shop's incentive is to make itself indispensable; without an internal technical authority, the shop can raise fees, withhold documentation, and block vendor substitution because the buyer cannot evaluate quality or alternatives.
bounded_by: does not apply when a company acquires an existing working software product and adds distribution on top of it

claims.text: Alex Hormozi spent approximately $1 million on an outsourced software development vendor for his AI lead-response product (Allen). The vendor progressively raised fees and refused to document the codebase, making the software impossible to hand off to another developer. The fees eventually consumed all margin.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: outsourced dev shop building proprietary software for a non-technical founder
claims.mechanism: Once a non-technical founder is operationally dependent on an outsourced dev shop, the shop holds a monopoly on the codebase and can extract economic rent by raising fees until margins are zero.

numbers.axis: software development spend vs. margin outcome

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's food business (meal delivery) generated $600,000 per month in revenue (60,000 meals at $10 each) at a net profit margin of approximately 7%. Supplementary analysis shows that 80% of customer support volume came from the food business while 90% of monthly profit came from his supplement line, which ran in parallel with the same support infrastructure.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: meal delivery business with $10 average meal price, $9 cost of goods

numbers.axis: revenue, margin, and support load by business line

bounded_by: 7% margin was achievable only because Hormozi ran a skeleton operation with pre-existing supplement infrastructure; without that, margins would have been negative

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that diverting a founder's attention from a high-margin core business to a new, lower-margin adjacent business is always more expensive than it appears, because the opportunity cost includes compound profit foregone on the original business. He estimates his food business cost him $10-25 million in lost Gym Launch exit value by reducing the profit base on which the acquisition multiple was calculated.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business sold on a profit multiple shortly after the distraction period
claims.mechanism: When a business is valued at a multiple of profit, every dollar of annual profit permanently subtracted through distraction multiplies into the exit price by the full transaction multiple.

anchors.value: $10-25 million (from $2-3M annual profit foregone multiplied by acquisition multiple)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi changed his Gym Launch membership price from $1,000 per week ($4,000/month) to $800 per week while simultaneously adding significant operational complexity (accountability groups, one-on-one support). He calculates that this reduced annual profit by approximately $5 million and that he never recovered the lost margin.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: membership business running at ~40% net margins
claims.mechanism: At 40% net margins, a 20% price reduction eliminates roughly 50% of net profit because the cost base is unchanged while top-line revenue drops proportionally; adding new delivery costs further compresses what remains.

numbers.axis: price change impact on annual profit

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that any pricing change — including a price decrease — produces customer complaints because customers dislike change itself, not just price increases. When he lowered prices for all existing members, the first reaction was a complaint that he had been overcharging them.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Customers interpret any pricing change as evidence that the prior price was wrong, which retroactively damages trust regardless of whether the change favors them.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that competing primarily by watching and reacting to competitors' moves is a strategic error; instead, founders should focus on customers, because solving customer problems renders competitors irrelevant. He attributes a version of this to Paul Graham: every core business problem can be solved by talking to customers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Competitors optimize for differentiation from each other, not for customer value; a company that optimizes solely for customer value will naturally outpace competitors without needing to track them.
bounded_by: finance problems (e.g., accounting, compliance) require financial specialists, not customer conversations

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that if someone is not living up to their potential at a job — coasting, avoiding challenges, watching the clock — they are incurring a double cost: the financial cost of foregone earnings development and the psychological cost of eroding self-concept. Leaving is superior to tolerating the environment, regardless of financial risk.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: person has the option to leave
claims.mechanism: Sustained misalignment between capability and challenge produces learned helplessness and self-concept damage that compounds into lower ambition and performance in subsequent endeavors.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi holds that vendor references are insufficient vetting. A vendor who is endorsed by a mutual contact must still be evaluated from scratch with specific-use-case references — people who have used that vendor for the same type of project at the same scale. He frames even strong personal referrals as zero-weight starting points.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: vendor engagement where failure would be catastrophic
claims.mechanism: Vendors lie to obtain association with large brands for resume-building purposes; personal referrals do not transfer use-case validation because the referrer's experience differs in scale, complexity, or type from the buyer's needs.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi spent $270,000 on a vendor for a product launch specifically as insurance against volume-handling failures. The vendor failed to handle the traffic: 75% of launch traffic did not reach the target destination, resulting in approximately $15 million in lost revenue.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: large-scale product launch with concentrated revenue window
claims.mechanism: The vendor misrepresented capability to win the contract for brand association; without use-case-matched references, the misrepresentation was undetectable in advance.

numbers.axis: vendor insurance spend vs. launch outcome

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when there is advance bad news about a vendor or partner situation — early warning signals that something is wrong — the eventual damage is always worse than the pre-event downside estimate. Suppressing bad news in order to avoid the near-term disruption of switching vendors or partners is a predictably costly mistake.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Organizations facing a bad-news situation are incentivized to minimize its severity to preserve the relationship and avoid work; the realized loss always exceeds the pre-revelation estimate because the full scope becomes visible only after failure.

examples.text: In 2017 Alex Hormozi was about to purchase $1 million of Ethereum at $100 per unit. Just before clicking purchase the price dipped to $93 and he pulled back. Ethereum subsequently appreciated roughly 30x from that entry level. Years later, near Bitcoin's 2021 peak of $60,000, he and a friend each put in $1 million; they lost approximately $500,000 in weeks. He uses both events to illustrate operating outside one's sphere of competence and acting on FOMO.

Hormozi's first real estate purchase was a house in Ohio for $50,000. The seller had bought it for $19,000 and done zero renovation. The house had no real electricity (drawing power illegally from a neighbor), a non-functional driveway requiring $7,000 to repair, and a bedroom-in-a-closet misrepresented as a third bedroom. Rent was $700/month, which did not cover even the driveway repair. Hormozi had to pay for the tenant's hotel stay during a month of repairs and ultimately sold the property for approximately $20,000. He was making $50,000 per day in profit at the time, making the time and energy cost far more damaging than the dollar loss.

Hormozi's first gym partner was recommended by an advisor who suggested splitting a gym 45-45-10 with someone who had an identical skillset and identical business. Both partners brought the same thing: labor and a fitness business. Within the partnership, neither had what the other lacked, making the split economically irrational from day one. This is the example Hormozi uses to illustrate that same-skillset partnerships are the worst possible structure.

After his Huntington Beach gym was generating $20,000-$25,000 per month in profit from a warehouse opened for $37,000, Hormozi opened a second location as a retail anchor tenant in a 7,000 sq ft space at $250,000 in opening costs. The second location produced identical monthly revenue. He later used this to illustrate that premium facilities do not automatically produce premium economics and that ROIC, not aesthetics, should govern spending.

A gym owner approached Hormozi during his Gym Launch consulting period and proposed a joint venture: the gym owner would manage operations after Hormozi ran the launch, giving Hormozi a path to own the gyms rather than just consulting. Hormozi agreed to personally guarantee the lease, fund the new location, run the launch, and hold half the equity while the partner would contribute operational management. After a launch that brought in approximately 370 new members and generated substantial cash, Hormozi deposited the proceeds into the joint LLC account. One morning the account was nearly zeroed by a single withdrawal the partner made to himself, claiming his half. The partner had been previously indicted for fraud; Hormozi knew this and gave him the benefit of the doubt. The partner sent the money to his girlfriend in Sweden and filed for bankruptcy to make recovery impossible.

Hormozi's AI lead-response product (Allen) achieved a 19% lead-to-visit conversion rate compared to the 10% baseline of a typical front-desk employee, validating the product hypothesis. However, the outsourced dev shop that built it progressively raised fees, refused to document the code, and eventually consumed all margin. Hormozi was unable to switch vendors or hire in-house developers because no one could read the undocumented codebase. He eventually sold the software to a company that did have in-house developers capable of reverse-engineering it.

At Gym Launch, Hormozi delegated compliance to his internal team. The team hired an external law firm to review all marketing content and training materials at rates of $150-$500/hour. Four lawyers watched every call and training and held bi-weekly meetings. The notes they produced were never read by anyone inside the company. Hormozi's CFO Suzanne flagged the $120,000/month legal spend on her first month in the role, informing him it was equivalent to full-scale litigation. She saved him approximately $1 million per year by terminating the arrangement.

Hormozi's meal delivery business (food company built on gym/supplement distribution) generated $600,000 per month at roughly $10/meal with $9 COGS. He ran it on a skeleton operation and still achieved only ~7% net margin. 80% of customer support volume came from food; 90% of monthly profit came from supplements. He estimates the opportunity cost of the food business — diverting attention from his supplement and gym business — at $10-25 million in foregone exit value when Gym Launch was sold at a profit multiple.

After a competitor began poaching Gym Launch's top gyms and undercutting on price, Hormozi reacted by adding a large accountability layer (35 elite gyms segmented by revenue, paired with peer groups one level ahead) while simultaneously cutting his price from $1,000/week to $800/week. The first customer response was a complaint that he had been overcharging previously. The price cut reduced annual profit by approximately $5 million. He was unable to recover that margin before selling the company, costing him the multiple-amplified value of $5M in annual profit lost.

practices.text: Before entering any investment outside your core domain of expertise, require that the person recommending the deal has been in the deal for at least two to three years.
When co-investing with an operator, insist on co-investing only in deals where the operator is also personally holding the same risk position as you.
When FOMO arises about an investment or business opportunity, treat the feeling itself as a signal to pause — not to act.
Ensure that every founder actively working in a business receives market-rate compensation as an employee, separate from and in addition to any equity position.
For every line item on a business expense report, be able to articulate a specific revenue return; if you cannot, treat the expense as a candidate for elimination.
Know the active problems in every department at least one level below your direct reports — not just whether things are going well, but what specific issues are being worked on.

When vetting a vendor, even one referred by a trusted contact, treat the referral as zero-weight and require use-case-matched references from clients who ran the same type of project at the same scale.

If building a software product, find a technical co-founder or technical equity partner before engaging any external development vendor; do not outsource core value generation without internal technical oversight.
Talk to customers — not competitors — when facing core business problems; customer conversations surface the actual constraint while competitor-watching surfaces noise.
When someone shows you who they are — through a red flag, a prior indictment, or a moment of dishonesty — believe them the first time and act accordingly.
